--- marp: true theme: uic-cs size: 16:9 paginate: true title: "AI as a Security Teammate" author: Kenan Alghythee --- # CS 487: Building Secure Computer Systems ## AI as a Security Teammate: *finding, fixing, and not trusting* bugs ### Fall 2026 Kenan Alghythee · SysSec group, UIC --- ## Today's plan | Time | Topic | Hands-on | |---|---|---| | 0–5 | Why this lecture exists | iClicker 1 | | 5–18 | Agents, and who is already using them for security | | | 18–30 | Why the human stays in the loop (theory + evidence) | iClicker 2 | | 30–58 | **Station 1:** static analysis + agent find & fix, then break the fix | you | | 58–70 | **Station 2 / 3:** agent reads packets · agent drives Ghidra | demo | | 70–75 | What to take into your next lab | iClicker 3 | Everything in `lab/` works in the SEED VM. Pair up; one laptop runs the agent, one verifies. --- ## Q1 · Which of these actually happened? **A.** An AI agent deleted a company's production database during a code freeze **B.** An AI found a memory-safety bug in SQLite that fuzzing had missed **C.** An AI agent topped a bug-bounty leaderboard against human hackers **D.** All of the above --- ## Q1 → **D. All of the above** %% TODO-REF: fill in dates/sources from research agent - **Replit, July 2025:** agent ignored a code freeze and dropped a production database, then described what it did as a "catastrophic error in judgment" - **Google Big Sleep, Nov 2024:** found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before release - **XBOW, 2025:** an autonomous pentester reached #1 on HackerOne's US leaderboard > Same technology, both sides of the ledger. This lecture is about how to get the second and third without the first. --- # Part 1 · Agents What an "agentic tool" is, and who is already pointing one at security --- ## From chatbot to agent
### One-shot LLM - You paste code, it returns text - No way to check its own answer - Wrong once, wrong forever
* ### Agent = LLM in a loop - **Observe:** read files, crash logs, tool output - **Plan:** decide what to try - **Act:** edit, compile, run, call a tool - **Verify:** did it work? loop again * ### Tools make the difference - Shell, compiler, debugger, sanitizer - **MCP** servers: Ghidra, Wireshark, CodeQL, a browser - Claude Code, Codex CLI, Copilot agent, Cursor, Aider
--- ## The same loop, three places in security | | Observe | Act | Verify | |---|---|---|---| | **Finding** | analyzer alarms, fuzzer crashes, diffs | write a harness, a checker, a query | reproduce the crash | | **Fixing** | sanitizer report, stack trace, PoC | edit the code | rebuild, replay PoC, run tests | | **Analysis** | packets, a stripped binary | decompile, filter, rename | ask a human |
Notice the last column. For finding, the verifier is a **crash** (ground truth). For fixing, it is a **test** (not ground truth). For analysis, it is **you**.
--- ## Who is already doing this · big labs and government %% TODO-REF: numbers from research agent
* ### Google - **Big Sleep** (Project Zero + DeepMind): SQLite bug, Nov 2024; more in 2025 - **OSS-Fuzz + LLM harnesses:** 26 new bugs, incl. a 20-year-old OpenSSL flaw - **AI-powered patching:** fixed ~15% of sanitizer bugs in production pipeline * ### OpenAI, Anthropic - **Aardvark** (Oct 2025): agentic security researcher - **Claude** security announcements, 2025–26
* ### DARPA AIxCC (final Aug 2025) - Teams built fully autonomous "cyber reasoning systems" - Finals: 54 synthetic vulns found, 43 patched, **18 real** bugs found along the way - Winners: Team Atlanta, Trail of Bits, Theori - Most systems open-sourced * ### Where I fit - Led the repair-stage work on Team Atlanta's winning system: ~20% higher repair accuracy, up to 50% fewer tokens
--- ## Who is already doing this · startups %% TODO-REF: verify list from research agent
### Finding - **XBOW** — autonomous pentesting - **Qwiet AI** — commercial Joern (code property graphs) + AI - **Semgrep Assistant** — triage + autofix - **ZeroPath, Corgea, Aisle** — LLM-native SAST
### Fixing & consulting - **Trail of Bits** — Buttercup (AIxCC), audits - **Theori** — Xint, AIxCC - **Pixee** — auto-remediation PRs - **Snyk DeepCode**
### Securing the AI - **Lakera, HiddenLayer, Protect AI** — prompt injection, model supply chain - **Socket** — malicious packages - Every one of the above also has to defend its own agent
Vibe-coding platforms (**Lovable**, **Replit**, Bolt) are on both sides: they ship AI-written code at scale, and their incidents are the case studies. --- ## Two cautionary tales from the vibe-coding world %% TODO-REF: confirm Lovable story from research agent
### Lovable, 2025 - Apps generated with default Supabase settings shipped **without row-level security** - A researcher scanned published apps and found user data readable by anyone - Lovable's response: an AI security scanner that reviews generated apps before publish
### Replit, July 2025 - Agent told repeatedly: code freeze, do not touch production - It ran a destructive migration anyway, then fabricated test results - Replit's response: separate dev/prod databases, one-click restore, planning-only mode
> The fix in both cases was not a better model. It was a **guardrail the model cannot talk its way past**. --- # Part 2 · Why the human stays in the loop Theory first, then the numbers --- ## Bug, vulnerability, patch - A **bug** is behavior the program was not supposed to have - A **vulnerability** is a bug an attacker can use to break confidentiality, integrity, or availability - A **patch** is a change that is supposed to remove the vulnerability and nothing else Three outcomes for a patch: | | The PoC input... | Other inputs... | |---|---|---| | Implausible | still crashes | | | **Plausible** | no longer crashes | may still trigger the bug, or now break | | Correct | no longer crashes | all intended behavior preserved, bug gone on every path | --- ## Can a machine decide "correct"?
**Rice's theorem (1953).** Every non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. "This program never writes out of bounds" is a semantic property. So is "this patch preserves every intended behavior". **Consequence.** No algorithm, and no model, can take an arbitrary program and patch and return *correct* / *incorrect* for all inputs.
**What machines can do:** - say *incorrect* when they find a counterexample (a crash, a failing test) - say *correct* for a **bounded** claim: this path, these inputs, this depth **What they cannot do:** - turn "all my tests pass" into "the bug is gone"
Same reason a fuzzer can only prove presence, never absence. Static analysis buys soundness by over-approximating, which is why it cries wolf.
%% TODO-REF: cite Rice 1953 + a textbook statement --- ## The models are not even deterministic %% TODO-REF: fill from research agent (nondeterminism paper) - Same model, same file, same prompt, run twice: **different bug lists** - Ullah et al. (IEEE S&P 2024): LLMs cannot reliably identify and reason about security vulnerabilities (yet?) - PrimeVul (ICSE 2025): on a realistic benchmark, code LLMs barely beat chance at vulnerability detection
**You will see this today.** When you compare patches with the pair next to you at Station 1, do not be surprised if they differ. The question is not "which one is right?" but "how would you know?"
--- ## Evidence 1 · The crash is not where the fix goes
**ARVO** (6,138 reproducible OSS-Fuzz bugs): - Fix location ≠ crash location in **~63%** of bugs - 1,789 fixes are in a **different file** than the crash - Only **~26%** are patched at a location that appears in the crash log Our analysis of ARVO v3; Kumushi (2026) reports ~40% of fixes outside the crash stack.
**PatchBench** (Sept 2026, 11 agents): - **81%** of the top agent's patches touch a function on the crash stack - When the developer's fix was off the stack, **64%** of agent patches still landed on it - Top failure mode (41 of 81): a narrow guard near the crash that misses other routes to the same bug
> The agent stops when *the one PoC* stops crashing. That is exactly a plausible patch. --- ## Evidence 2 · What we measured (CARO, 2026)
**Setup.** Coding agents (Qwen3 27B, Claude Sonnet 4.6) repair 97 real ARVO memory-safety bugs in Docker. We vary the hint (none, crash frame, true fix location, wrong location) and whether the agent sees execution feedback. **Judging.** Rebuild, replay PoC, replay seeds, fuzz, then an LLM-judge panel plus human audit.
* **Pointing matters.** Telling the agent *where* raises agreement with the maintainer's fix from 39% → 60% (Sonnet). The crash resolution rate does not move. * **Feedback helps a bit.** Crash resolution 38% → 47% with execution feedback, statistically inconclusive. * **Half the "fixes" are symptom suppression.** 52% of Sonnet's unguided crash-resolving patches silence the crash without fixing the bug.
--- ## Evidence 3 · Where the teammate model works
### LLM proposes, analyzer and fuzzer confirm - LLM writes **Clang Static Analyzer checkers** from past CVE patches - Analyzer path conditions steer a **directed fuzzer** - Only a reproduced crash counts **Result:** 33 bugs, 22 reported, 12 fixes merged in FFmpeg, 3 CVEs (two bugs latent for 12 years), plus libxml2, open62541, Mosquitto, Fluent Bit
### Agent learns from human review - **PatchAdvisor:** 6,946 syzbot kernel fix lifecycles, including mailing-list revisions - Fine-tuned advisor steers the coding agent toward patches **maintainers accept**, not just patches that compile ### The bottleneck is not finding - **SoK, IEEE S&P 2027:** kernel bug discovery (syzbot) far outpaces triage, patching, and validation
Alghythee et al., FFmpeg CVE-2026-52295/52296/52297 · Bai, Alghythee, Zhang, Wang, arXiv:2604.03851 · Bai, She, Alghythee, Zhang, Wang, IEEE S&P 2027 --- ## Q2 · An agent patches a stack overflow by replacing `strcpy` with `strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst)`. The crash input no longer crashes. The patch is: **A.** Correct **B.** Plausible but incorrect **C.** Implausible **D.** Can't tell without more information --- ## Q2 → **B. Plausible but incorrect** (and D is a fair answer) ```c char name[32]; strncpy(name, src, sizeof name); /* 32-byte src -> no terminating NUL */ printf("name=%s\n", name); /* reads past name into the next field */ ``` - The crash is gone. The overflow is gone. The **information leak** is new. - To call it *correct* you would need to know every reader of `name`. That is the semantic property Rice says you can't decide in general; you can only check the readers you can find. > You are about to make an agent write this exact patch. --- # Part 3 · Hands-on Station 1 is yours. Stations 2 and 3 are on the projector. --- ## Station 1 · Find, fix, then break the fix
**You get:** `recparse.c`, a 100-line record-file parser with bugs, five test inputs, and `check.sh`. **Steps** (28 min, in pairs): 1) Build and run `./check.sh` — three FAILs 2) Run **cppcheck**, **flawfinder**, Semgrep if Docker works. Count findings. 3) Give the agent the code **and the analyzer output**. "Find every memory-safety bug and fix it." 4) `./check.sh` again. Then run `leak-name32.bin` and *read the name*. 5) Write one new input you think the patched program mishandles.
```sh cd lab/station1-find-and-fix make inputs && make && ./check.sh cppcheck --enable=warning,style recparse.c flawfinder recparse.c export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # class key claude ```
**Record:** analyzer findings vs. real bugs · did the first patch pass? · does your neighbor's patch match yours?
--- ## Station 1 · What the analyzers say ``` recparse.c:48: (warning) strcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows [flawfinder, CWE-120] recparse.c:63: (warning) memcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows [flawfinder, CWE-120] recparse.c:29: (style) Variable 'buf' can be declared as pointer to const [cppcheck] ``` - flawfinder flags **every** `strcpy` and `memcpy`: one true positive, one real but for a reason it doesn't know - cppcheck's one hit is irrelevant - Nobody flagged the **signed comparison** `len > MAX_DATA` where `len` is `int32_t` and can be negative > This is the division of labor: the analyzer is loud and sound-ish, the model is quiet and plausible, and the input file is the only judge. --- ## Station 1 · Debrief
* **Did the first patch pass `check.sh`?** Usually. Did it pass `leak-name32`? Often not. If it did, how do you know the next input won't? * **Did neighbors get the same patch?** Rarely identical. Same model, same prompt. Different fix locations, different guards. * **Step 5: what did you try?** `len == MAX_DATA` · file ends inside the length · empty file · no NUL anywhere
**What a test suite is.** A finite set of counterexample searches. It can prove *incorrect*. It cannot prove *correct*. Neither can the agent, no matter how confidently it reports "all tests pass". **What you did** that the agent could not: decided which property mattered (no leak, not just no crash) and wrote the input that checks it.
--- ## Station 2 · An agent reads packets
**Capture:** `lab/station2-packets/demo.pcap`, 44 frames, synthetic. **Prompts** (you drive, students call them out): 1. "Summarize this capture. Who talks to whom?" 2. "Is there anything a security reviewer should flag?" 3. "Decode the Authorization header." 4. "Which host is scanning, and what did it learn?" **Then:** "Which of these findings would you have gotten from a Wireshark display filter in 10 seconds?"
```sh tshark -r demo.pcap -q -z conv,tcp tshark -r demo.pcap -Y http -T fields \ -e ip.src -e http.request.line claude # with tshark in PATH ``` * **What the agent is good at:** turning 44 frames into three sentences, decoding, suggesting the next filter * **What it is not:** seeing anything `tshark` didn't print. It reads text, not bytes. * **The twist:** a frame in this capture contains text addressed to the agent. Watch whether it obeys.
--- ## Station 3 · An agent drives Ghidra
**Binary:** `lab/station3-ghidra/keycheck`, stripped, PIE, x86-64. Accepts a license key or rejects it. **Prompts:** 1. "What does this program check?" 2. "Describe the key format and the validation function." 3. "Is there any way in besides a valid key?" 4. "Rename the functions and variables to match what they do." **Then:** "The agent found the second way in. Should it exist? Who would you ask?"
* ### Setup (before class) - Ghidra 11+, **GhidraMCP** plugin (or GhidrAssist) - `claude mcp add ghidra ...`, import `keycheck`, auto-analyze * ### What to watch for - It names `check_key` correctly from the hash constants (FNV-1a) - It finds the string compare on the second path - It will **confidently** describe the hash; make it show the decompiled line - Ask it for a valid key. It will offer to brute-force. `findkey.py` already did.
--- # Part 4 · What to take with you The teammate contract --- ## The contract
### The agent's job - Read more than you have time to - Propose: a finding, a patch, a filter, a name - Run the cheap checks: build, replay, tests - Say what it did, in a form you can replay
### Your job - Decide **which property** matters (no crash? no leak? no behavior change?) - Write the input that checks it - Treat "all tests pass" as the start of review, not the end - Keep a guardrail the agent cannot argue with: a sanitizer, a PoC, a prod database it cannot reach
> Undecidability is not a reason to avoid the tools. It is the reason the loop needs a human in it, and the reason you now know where to stand. --- ## Q3 · Your agent reports "fixed, all 5 tests pass" on Lab 3's format-string bug. What's your next move? **A.** Merge it; the tests pass **B.** Ask the agent to confirm the fix is correct **C.** Write the input the tests don't cover, then read the diff **D.** Run it again to see if it gives the same patch --- ## Q3 → **C. Write the uncovered input, then read the diff** - **A** trusts a finite test suite to decide an undecidable property - **B** asks the proposer to be the judge - **D** tells you the model is unstable, not whether this patch is right - **C** is what you did at Station 1, and it is the whole lecture --- ## References
**Theory** - Rice, "Classes of recursively enumerable sets and their decision problems," Trans. AMS, 1953 - Qi, Long, Achour, Rinard, "An analysis of patch plausibility and correctness," ISSTA 2015 - Smith, Barr, Le Goues, Brun, "Is the cure worse than the disease? Overfitting in automated program repair," FSE 2015 %% TODO-REF: nondeterminism paper - Ullah et al., "LLMs cannot reliably identify and reason about security vulnerabilities (yet?)," IEEE S&P 2024 - Ding et al., "Vulnerability detection with code language models: how far are we?" (PrimeVul), ICSE 2025 **Data** - ARVO: arxiv.org/abs/2408.02153 - PatchBench: arxiv.org/abs/2609.04075 - Kumushi: arxiv.org/abs/2605.04251 - Google, "AI-powered patching," 2024
**Our work** - Alghythee et al., "Pointed at the Crash" (CARO), under submission, 2026 - Bai, Alghythee, Zhang, Wang, "Beyond Crash-to-Patch" (PatchAdvisor), arxiv.org/abs/2604.03851 - Bai, She, Alghythee, Zhang, Wang, "SoK: From Finding to Deployment," IEEE S&P 2027 - FFmpeg CVE-2026-52295, -52296, -52297 **Industry** %% TODO-REF: fill URLs - Google Project Zero, "From naptime to Big Sleep," Nov 2024 - DARPA AIxCC final results, DEF CON 33, Aug 2025 - Replit / SaaStr incident, July 2025 - Lovable security scanner announcement, 2025 **Lab materials:** `lab/` in this repo

cat > lab/README.md <<'EOF'
# Lab materials · AI as a Security Teammate (CS 487)

Three stations. Station 1 is for students. Stations 2 and 3 are instructor
demos by default; each has a runbook so either can be student-driven.

| Station | Directory | What happens | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `station1-find-and-fix/` | static analysis + agent finds and patches `recparse.c`, students break the patch | gcc, Claude Code, flawfinder (optional cppcheck, Semgrep) |
| 2 | `station2-packets/` | agent summarizes and questions a pcap | tshark, Claude Code |
| 3 | `station3-ghidra/` | agent drives Ghidra on a stripped binary | Ghidra 12.1.4, GhidraMCP, Claude Code |

## Setup in the SEED VM (Ubuntu 20.04)

**Claude Code.** The native installer needs no Node.js and lists Ubuntu 20.04 as
supported. Smoke-test on one VM before class.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
claude --version
```

If `claude` segfaults on the 20.04 glibc, pin an older build:
`curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash -s 2.1.245`.

**Class key.** Each student runs, in the shell where they start `claude`:

```sh
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # handed out in class
claude
```

Claude Code asks once whether to use the key from the environment; answer yes
and it skips the login prompt. Create the key in the Anthropic Console with the
"Claude Code" role, set a spend limit, and revoke it after the lecture.

**Analyzers.**

```sh
pip3 install flawfinder            # works on Python 3.8
sudo apt install -y cppcheck tshark
# Semgrep needs Python 3.10+, so use Docker in the SEED VM:
docker pull semgrep/semgrep
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/src" semgrep/semgrep semgrep scan --config p/c
```

**Ghidra (station 3 only).** Ghidra 12.1.4 from github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/releases,
then the GhidraMCP 2.0 extension zip from github.com/LaurieWired/GhidraMCP/releases:
File → Install Extensions → + → pick the zip → restart Ghidra → File → Configure →
Developer → enable GhidraMCPPlugin. Then register the server with Claude Code:

```sh
pip3 install uv     # or pipx; GhidraMCP's Python side wants 3.10+, uv fetches one
claude mcp add ghidra -- uvx --from git+https://github.com/LaurieWired/GhidraMCP ghidra-mcp --ghidra-server http://127.0.0.1:8080/
```

Fallback if MCP misbehaves on the day: in Ghidra, export the decompiled C
(File → Export Program → C/C++) and hand that file to Claude Code. Same
prompts, same lesson.

## Before class checklist

- [ ] `claude --version` works in the SEED VM
- [ ] Class key created, spend limit set, copied somewhere you can read aloud
- [ ] `cd lab/station1-find-and-fix && make inputs && make && ./check.sh` shows 3 FAIL
- [ ] `tshark -r lab/station2-packets/demo.pcap -q -z conv,tcp` prints 4 conversations
- [ ] `lab/station3-ghidra/keycheck` built and imported into Ghidra, auto-analysis done
- [ ] Projector laptop has `claude` logged in with your own account, not the class key

cat > lab/station2-packets/README.md <<'EOF'
# Station 2 · An agent reads packets

`demo.pcap` is synthetic (generated by `mkpcap.py`, no dependencies). It
holds 44 frames: a DNS lookup, a cleartext HTTP login, an HTTP request with
a Basic authorization header, and a SYN sweep from a third host against 14
ports on the server. Addresses are private (10.9.0.0/24, the Lab 3 subnet).

## Runbook (10 min)

```sh
cd lab/station2-packets
tshark -r demo.pcap -q -z conv,tcp          # four TCP conversations
tshark -r demo.pcap -Y http -T fields -e ip.src -e http.request.line
claude
```

Prompts, in order. Let the students call out the next one.

1. "Summarize demo.pcap. Who talks to whom, and over what?"
2. "Is there anything a security reviewer should flag?"
3. "Decode the Authorization header in the GET /admin request."
4. "One host sends SYNs to many ports. Which ports answered, and what does that tell an attacker?"
5. "Write me the Wireshark display filter that shows only the suspicious traffic."

Then ask the room: which of these would a display filter have shown in ten
seconds, and which needed the model? Expected answer: the model is good at
the summary and at proposing the next filter; everything it "found" is a
string `tshark` already printed. It cannot see bytes `tshark` did not decode.

## If you want the agent to call tshark as a tool

Claude Code's shell tool is enough for this demo. For a tool-shaped setup,
`bx33661/Wireshark-MCP` on PyPI (`wireshark-mcp`, Python 3.10+) wraps tshark
as an MCP server. There is no official Wireshark MCP integration as of Nov 2026.

## Regenerating

`python3 mkpcap.py` rewrites `demo.pcap`. Edit the hosts, credentials, or
port list at the top of the script.

cat > lab/station3-ghidra/README.md <<'EOF'
# Station 3 · An agent drives Ghidra

`keycheck` is a stripped, PIE x86-64 binary built from `keycheck.c`. It
accepts a 12-character license key of the form `XXXX-XXXX-XX`, validated
with an FNV-1a hash, and also accepts one hard-coded support key.
`findkey.py` brute-forces a valid key so you have one ready.

```sh
make                      # builds ./keycheck (stripped)
python3 findkey.py        # prints a valid key, e.g. ABEL-UIC4-87
./keycheck ABEL-UIC4-87   # key accepted
```

## Runbook (10 min)

Before class: import `keycheck` into Ghidra 12.1.4, run auto-analysis, enable
GhidraMCP, register it with `claude mcp add ghidra ...` (see `../README.md`).

Prompts:

1. "What does this program check? Start from main."
2. "Describe the key format and the validation function in plain English."
3. "Is there any way to get 'key accepted' without a valid key?"
4. "Rename the functions and variables to match what they do."
5. "Give me a key that passes." (It will offer to brute-force. Let it, or show `findkey.py`.)

What to point out:

- It identifies FNV-1a from the two constants. Make it show the decompiled line, not just assert it.
- It finds the second accept path (a string compare). Ask the room: should this exist, and who would you ask? A model can find the backdoor; it cannot tell you whether it is authorized.
- Renaming is where the agent earns its keep: the decompiler output becomes readable in one prompt.

## Fallback

If MCP is flaky, export the decompiled C from Ghidra (File → Export Program →
C/C++) and give the file to Claude Code. Same prompts, same lesson.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate every figure for cs487-ai-security-teammate.md into this directory.
Charts: matplotlib -> SVG. Diagrams: hand-built SVG strings. Run: python3 make_figures.py
"""
import os
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import rcParams

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
BLUE, RED, GOLD = "#0A4FA3", "#D50032", "#C98A00"   # validated categorical set
NAVY, CYAN, GRAY, INK, TINT = "#001E62", "#00B5E2", "#656665", "#2b2b2b", "#f4f6fa"
LIGHT = "#d9dde6"

rcParams.update({
    "svg.fonttype": "none", "font.family": "sans-serif",
    "font.sans-serif": ["Helvetica Neue", "Helvetica", "Arial", "Liberation Sans"],
    "font.size": 15, "axes.edgecolor": LIGHT, "axes.linewidth": 1,
    "xtick.color": GRAY, "ytick.color": GRAY, "text.color": INK, "axes.labelcolor": GRAY,
})

def save(fig, name):
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(HERE, name), format="svg", bbox_inches="tight", transparent=True)
    plt.close(fig)

def clean(ax, left=True):
    for s in ("top", "right", "bottom"): ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(left)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)

def hbars(ax, labels, values, colors, vmax, fmt="{}", lw=0.62):
    y = list(range(len(labels)))[::-1]
    ax.barh(y, values, color=colors, height=lw)
    for yi, v in zip(y, values):
        ax.text(v + vmax * 0.015, yi, fmt.format(v), va="center", ha="left", fontsize=16, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_yticks(y); ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=15)
    ax.set_xlim(0, vmax * 1.18); ax.set_xticks([])
    clean(ax, left=False)

# ---------- charts ----------
def aixcc():
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 2]})
    hbars(axs[0], ["Synthetic vulns in the finals", "Found by at least one system", "Patched"],
          [63, 54, 43], [LIGHT, BLUE, BLUE], 63)
    axs[0].set_title("Seven autonomous systems, 63 planted bugs", loc="left", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
    hbars(axs[1], ["Real bugs found along the way", "Patched"], [18, 11], [RED, RED], 18)
    axs[1].set_title("Nobody planted these", loc="left", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
    save(fig, "aixcc.svg")

def bigsleep():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.6))
    hbars(ax, ["Big Sleep (LLM agent)", "Fuzzilli (fuzzer)"], [45, 37], [BLUE, GOLD], 45)
    ax.set_title("Bugs found in V8, Apr–Sep 2026 · ~25% overlap", loc="left", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
    save(fig, "bigsleep.svg")

def nondeterminism():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.8))
    hbars(ax, ["CodeContests", "APPS", "HumanEval"], [76, 51, 48], [BLUE] * 3, 76, fmt="{}%")
    ax.set_title("Tasks where 5 runs of the same prompt gave no two identical outputs", loc="left", fontsize=14, color=GRAY)
    save(fig, "nondeterminism.svg")

def passk():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.2))
    hbars(ax, ["1 attempt", "30 attempts"], [5, 33], [BLUE, BLUE], 33, fmt="{}%")
    ax.set_title("Chance of finding a new vulnerability (Claude Sonnet 4.5)", loc="left", fontsize=14, color=GRAY)
    save(fig, "passk.svg")

def location():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4))
    labels = ["Real fixes NOT at the crash location  (ARVO, 6,138 bugs)",
              "Real fixes at a location in the crash log  (ARVO)",
              "Agent patches ON the crash stack  (PatchBench, top agent)",
              "...still on the stack when the real fix was elsewhere"]
    hbars(ax, labels, [63, 26, 81, 64], [BLUE, BLUE, RED, RED], 81, fmt="{}%")
    save(fig, "location.svg")

def caro():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
    groups = ["Qwen3 27B", "Claude Sonnet 4.6"]
    none, hint = [35, 39], [53, 60]
    x = [0, 1]; w = 0.34
    b1 = ax.bar([i - w / 2 for i in x], none, w, color=LIGHT, label="No hint")
    b2 = ax.bar([i + w / 2 for i in x], hint, w, color=BLUE, label="Told where the fix goes")
    for bars in (b1, b2):
        for b in bars:
            ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, b.get_height() + 1.5, f"{int(b.get_height())}%", ha="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(groups, fontsize=15); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_ylim(0, 72)
    clean(ax, left=False)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_title("Patches at the maintainer's fix location", loc="left", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
    save(fig, "caro.svg")

def qi2015():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
    hbars(ax, ["Defects tried", "\"Repaired\" (tests pass)", "Actually correct"], [105, 55, 2], [LIGHT, BLUE, RED], 105)
    ax.set_title("GenProg on 105 real bugs (Qi et al., ISSTA 2015)", loc="left", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
    save(fig, "qi2015.svg")

# ---------- diagrams ----------
FONT = "font-family='Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif'"

def svg(w, h, body):
    return f"<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 {w} {h}' width='{w}' height='{h}' {FONT}>\n<defs><marker id='a' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='{GRAY}'/></marker></defs>\n{body}\n</svg>\n"

def box(x, y, w, h, title, sub="", fill=TINT, stroke=NAVY, tcol=NAVY, r=10, fs=22):
    t = f"<rect x='{x}' y='{y}' width='{w}' height='{h}' rx='{r}' fill='{fill}' stroke='{stroke}' stroke-width='2.5'/>"
    cy = y + h / 2 + (0 if not sub else -10)
    t += f"<text x='{x + w / 2}' y='{cy + 7}' text-anchor='middle' font-size='{fs}' font-weight='700' fill='{tcol}'>{title}</text>"
    if sub:
        t += f"<text x='{x + w / 2}' y='{cy + 32}' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' fill='{GRAY}'>{sub}</text>"
    return t

def arrow(x1, y1, x2, y2, label="", col=GRAY, dash=""):
    d = f" stroke-dasharray='{dash}'" if dash else ""
    t = f"<line x1='{x1}' y1='{y1}' x2='{x2}' y2='{y2}' stroke='{col}' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#a)'{d}/>"
    if label:
        t += f"<text x='{(x1 + x2) / 2}' y='{(y1 + y2) / 2 - 10}' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' fill='{GRAY}'>{label}</text>"
    return t

def text(x, y, s, fs=18, col=INK, anchor="start", bold=False):
    return f"<text x='{x}' y='{y}' font-size='{fs}' fill='{col}' text-anchor='{anchor}'{' font-weight=\"700\"' if bold else ''}>{s}</text>"

def write(name, content):
    open(os.path.join(HERE, name), "w").write(content)

def agent_loop():
    b = ""
    b += box(40, 60, 220, 90, "Observe", "files, crash logs, tool output")
    b += box(500, 60, 220, 90, "Plan", "decide what to try")
    b += box(500, 300, 220, 90, "Act", "edit · compile · run · call a tool")
    b += box(40, 300, 220, 90, "Verify", "did it work?", fill="#fde8ec", stroke=RED, tcol=RED)
    b += arrow(262, 105, 498, 105)
    b += arrow(610, 152, 610, 298)
    b += arrow(498, 345, 262, 345)
    b += arrow(150, 298, 150, 152, "loop")
    b += text(380, 230, "LLM", 26, NAVY, "middle", True)
    b += text(380, 258, "one model call per step", 15, GRAY, "middle")
    b += text(770, 90, "Tools it can call", 18, NAVY, "start", True)
    for i, t in enumerate(["shell, gcc, gdb, sanitizers", "tshark, Ghidra, CodeQL via MCP", "the test suite", "the production database"]):
        col = RED if i == 3 else INK
        b += text(770, 125 + i * 32, "• " + t, 17, col)
    b += text(770, 300, "The Verify step is where", 16, GRAY)
    b += text(770, 324, "the agent decides what", 16, GRAY)
    b += text(770, 348, "\"it worked\" means.", 16, GRAY)
    write("agent-loop.svg", svg(1080, 420, b))

def patch_sets():
    b = ""
    b += f"<ellipse cx='330' cy='210' rx='320' ry='190' fill='#eef2f8' stroke='{GRAY}' stroke-width='2'/>"
    b += f"<ellipse cx='300' cy='225' rx='215' ry='135' fill='#dbe6f6' stroke='{BLUE}' stroke-width='2.5'/>"
    b += f"<circle cx='250' cy='250' r='40' fill='{RED}' stroke='none'/>"
    b += text(330, 55, "Patches that stop the PoC crash", 19, GRAY, "middle", True)
    b += text(330, 78, "\"plausible\"", 16, GRAY, "middle")
    b += text(300, 125, "...that also pass every test", 19, BLUE, "middle", True)
    b += text(300, 148, "what the agent reports as done", 16, BLUE, "middle")
    b += text(250, 256, "correct", 17, "#fff", "middle", True)
    b += arrow(700, 300, 300, 268, col=RED)
    b += text(720, 290, "The thing you want.", 20, RED, "start", True)
    b += text(720, 318, "Rinard's group found it is", 17, INK)
    b += text(720, 342, "\"orders of magnitude\" less", 17, INK)
    b += text(720, 366, "common than the blue ring.", 17, INK)
    b += text(720, 110, "Implausible patches", 20, NAVY, "start", True)
    b += text(720, 138, "live outside the outer ring:", 17, INK)
    b += text(720, 162, "the PoC still crashes.", 17, INK)
    write("patch-sets.svg", svg(1080, 420, b))

def decide():
    import random
    random.seed(487)
    b = ""
    b += f"<rect x='40' y='40' width='620' height='340' rx='14' fill='#eef2f8' stroke='{GRAY}' stroke-width='2'/>"
    b += text(350, 70, "every possible input (infinite)", 17, GRAY, "middle")
    for _ in range(260):
        x, y = random.uniform(60, 640), random.uniform(90, 365)
        b += f"<circle cx='{x:.0f}' cy='{y:.0f}' r='3' fill='{LIGHT}'/>"

    b += arrow(522, 150, 598, 150, "patch")
    b += arrow(782, 140, 858, 90)
    b += arrow(782, 160, 858, 210)

--- marp: true theme: uic-cs size: 16:9 paginate: true title: "AI as a Security Teammate" author: Kenan Alghythee --- # CS 487: Building Secure Computer Systems ## AI as a Security Teammate: *find, fix, and don't trust* ### Fall 2026 Kenan Alghythee · SysSec group, UIC --- ## Today | | | | |---|---|---| | 0–5 | Why this lecture | iClicker 1 | | 5–18 | Agents, and who already uses them | | | 18–30 | Why the human stays in the loop | iClicker 2 | | 30–58 | **Station 1:** make an agent fix a bug, then break its fix | you | | 58–70 | **Station 2 / 3:** agent reads packets · agent drives Ghidra | demo | | 70–75 | The contract | iClicker 3 | --- ## Q1 · Which of these actually happened? **A.** An AI agent deleted a company's production database during a code freeze **B.** An AI found a memory-safety bug in SQLite that fuzzing had missed **C.** An AI agent topped a bug-bounty leaderboard against human hackers **D.** All of the above --- ## Q1 → **D. All of the above**
### Replit · Jul 2025 Code freeze. Agent dropped the production DB anyway, then misreported it.
### Big Sleep · Nov 2024 SQLite stack underflow. 150 CPU-hours of fuzzing had missed it.
### XBOW · Jun 2025 #1 on HackerOne's US leaderboard. ~1,060 reports, humans reviewed each.
> Same technology, both sides of the ledger. Today: how to get the second and third without the first. --- # Part 1 · Agents What an agentic tool is, and who is pointing one at security --- ## An agent is a model in a loop with tools ![w:1080](figures/agent-loop.svg) --- ## Same loop, three jobs, three different verifiers | | Observe | Act | Verify | |---|---|---|---| | **Finding** | analyzer alarms, fuzzer crashes | write a harness, a checker, a query | **a crash** | | **Fixing** | sanitizer report, PoC | edit the code | **a test** | | **Analysis** | packets, a stripped binary | decompile, filter, rename | **you** |
A crash is ground truth. A passing test is not. A person is the only verifier for "is this normal?"
--- ## Finding: the agents are real now
![w:520](figures/bigsleep.svg) Project Zero, "Fuzzers vs. AI," Oct 2026
- **Google Big Sleep:** SQLite 2024, 20 bugs in FFmpeg and ImageMagick 2025 - **Anthropic:** 500+ validated high-severity bugs; 22 in Firefox in two weeks - **OpenAI Codex Security:** 792 criticals in 1.2M commits - Every announcement says: *a human validated before reporting*
--- ## DARPA AIxCC: seven systems, no humans, two days ![w:1080](figures/aixcc.svg) Final at DEF CON 33, Aug 2025. 1st Team Atlanta, 2nd Trail of Bits, 3rd Theori. All seven systems are open source. I led the repair-stage work on Team Atlanta's system: ~20% more accurate, up to 50% fewer tokens. --- ## Who is selling this ![w:1080](figures/landscape.svg) --- ## Two cautionary tales from vibe-coding ![w:1080](figures/timeline.svg) > Neither fix was a better model. Both were a **guardrail the model cannot talk its way past**. --- # Part 2 · Why the human stays in the loop One theorem, one habit of the models, and three sets of numbers --- ## Three outcomes for a patch ![w:1080](figures/patch-sets.svg) --- ## "Tests pass" has never meant "fixed" ![w:900](figures/qi2015.svg) - Smith et al. (FSE 2015): the median GenProg patch that passes 100% of the training tests passes **83%** of held-out tests - Long & Rinard (ICSE 2016): wrong-but-passing patches are **orders of magnitude** more common than correct ones --- ## Can a machine decide "correct"? ![w:1080](figures/decide.svg) --- ## The models are not even deterministic
![w:520](figures/nondeterminism.svg) Ouyang et al., TOSEM 2024. Temperature 0 reduces it, does not remove it.
![w:520](figures/passk.svg) Anthropic, Sep 2025. Unreliable once, useful in bulk, *if someone checks*.
- Ullah et al. (S&P 2024): 228 vulnerable snippets, each asked 10 times. **Every** model changed its answer on some of them - You will see this at Station 1 when you compare patches with the next pair --- ## Evidence 1 · The crash is not where the fix goes ![w:1080](figures/location.svg) > The agent stops when *the one PoC* stops crashing. That is the definition of a plausible patch. --- ## Evidence 2 · What we measured (CARO, 2026)
![w:520](figures/caro.svg)
**97 real OSS-Fuzz bugs**, agents in Docker, patches checked by rebuild, PoC replay, fuzzing, and human audit. - Pointing helps the *location*. Crash resolution does not move. - Execution feedback: 38% → 47%, inconclusive.
**52%** of Sonnet's unguided crash-resolving patches are **symptom suppression**.
--- ## Evidence 3 · Where the teammate model works ![w:1080](figures/pipeline.svg) - **PatchAdvisor:** learn from 6,946 kernel fix histories what maintainers *accept* - **SoK (S&P 2027):** finding outpaces triage, patching, and validation. The bottleneck is the human part. --- ## Q2 · The agent replaces `strcpy` with `strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst)`. The crash input no longer crashes. The patch is: **A.** Correct **B.** Plausible but incorrect **C.** Implausible **D.** Can't tell without more information --- ## Q2 → **B** (and D is a fair answer) ```c char name[32]; strncpy(name, src, sizeof name); /* 32-byte src -> no terminating NUL */ printf("name=%s\n", name); /* reads past name into the next field */ ``` - Crash gone. Overflow gone. **Information leak** is new. - "Correct" needs every reader of `name`. You can check the ones you can find. > You are about to make an agent write this exact patch. --- # Part 3 · Hands-on Station 1 is yours. Stations 2 and 3 are on the projector. --- ## Station 1 · Find, fix, then break the fix ![w:1080](figures/station1.svg) ```sh cd lab/station1-find-and-fix && make inputs && make && ./check.sh # 3 FAIL flawfinder recparse.c ; cppcheck --enable=warning,style recparse.c export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # class key, revoked after class claude ``` --- ## Station 1 · What the analyzers say ``` $ gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c recparse.c # silent $ flawfinder --dataonly recparse.c recparse.c:47: [4] strcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows (CWE-120) recparse.c:21: [2] char: Statically-sized arrays can be improperly restricted recparse.c:28: [2] fopen: Check when opening files - can an attacker redirect it recparse.c:53: [2] memcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows (CWE-120) recparse.c:63: [2] memcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows (CWE-120) ``` | line | verdict | |---|---| | 47 | ✓ the bug it says it is | | 63 | ✓ a bug, but the cause is a **signed** `len` check six lines up | | 21, 28, 53 | ✗ noise | --- ## Station 1 · Debrief
* **First patch passed `check.sh`?** Usually. Passed `leak-name32`? Often not. * **Neighbor got the same patch?** Rarely. Same model, same prompt. * **Your 6th input?** `len == MAX_DATA` · truncated length · empty file · no NUL
A test suite is a finite set of counterexample searches. It proves *incorrect*. It cannot prove *correct*. **You** chose the property (no leak, not just no crash) and wrote the input. The agent cannot do that part.
--- ## Station 2 · An agent reads packets ![w:1080](figures/network.svg) --- ## Station 3 · An agent drives Ghidra ![w:1080](figures/ghidra.svg) --- # Part 4 · The contract What the agent does, what you do, and what neither gets to skip --- ## The contract ![w:1080](figures/contract.svg) > Undecidability is not a reason to avoid the tools. It is the reason the loop needs a human, and now you know where to stand. --- ## Q3 · Your agent says "fixed, all 5 tests pass" on Lab 3's format-string bug. Next move? **A.** Merge it; the tests pass **B.** Ask the agent to confirm the fix is correct **C.** Write the input the tests don't cover, then read the diff **D.** Run it again and see if it gives the same patch --- ## Q3 → **C. Write the uncovered input, then read the diff** - **A** trusts a finite test suite to decide an undecidable property - **B** asks the proposer to be the judge - **D** tells you the model is unstable, not whether this patch is right - **C** is what you did at Station 1 --- ## References
**Theory & data** - Rice, Trans. AMS, 1953 · Al-Bataineh, ICSE 2026 NIER - Qi, Long, Achour, Rinard, ISSTA 2015 · Smith, Barr, Le Goues, Brun, FSE 2015 · Long & Rinard, ICSE 2016 - Ullah et al., IEEE S&P 2024 · Ouyang, Zhang, Harman, Wang, TOSEM 2024 · He et al., Thinking Machines, 2025 - Ding et al. (PrimeVul), ICSE 2025 - ARVO arXiv:2408.02153 · PatchBench arXiv:2609.04075 · Kumushi arXiv:2605.04251 - Google, "AI-powered patching," 2024 · Anthropic, "Building AI for cyber defenders," Sep 2025 **Our work** - Alghythee et al., "Pointed at the Crash" (CARO), under submission 2026 - Bai, Alghythee, Zhang, Wang, "Beyond Crash-to-Patch," arXiv:2604.03851 - Bai, She, Alghythee, Zhang, Wang, "SoK: From Finding to Deployment," IEEE S&P 2027 - FFmpeg CVE-2026-52295 / 52296 / 52297
**Industry** - Project Zero, "From Naptime to Big Sleep," Nov 2024; "Fuzzers vs. AI," Oct 2026 - DARPA, AIxCC final results, Aug 2025 - Anthropic, "LLM-discovered 0-days," Feb 2026; "Project Glasswing," Apr 2026 - OpenAI, "Introducing Aardvark," Oct 2025; "Codex Security," Mar 2026 - XBOW, "The road to top 1," Jun 2025 - Palmer, CVE-2025-48757, May 2025 · Lovable, "Swarms of AI hacking agents," Jul 2026 - Replit, "A safer way to vibe code," Jul 2025 · The Register, Jul 22, 2025 **Lab materials:** `lab/` in this repo. Figures: `slides/figures/make_figures.py`
--- # Questions? ### Thank you Kenan Alghythee · kalghy2@uic.edu

The patch is: **A.** Correct **B.** Plausible but incorrect **C.** Implausible **D.** Can't tell without more information --- ## Q2 → **B** (and D is a fair answer) ```c char name[32]; strncpy(name, src, sizeof name); /* 32-byte src -> no terminating NUL */ printf("name=%s\n", name); /* reads past name into the next field */ ``` - Crash gone. Overflow gone. **Information leak** is new. - "Correct" needs every reader of `name`. You can check the ones you can find. > You are about to make an agent write this exact patch. --- # Part 3 · Hands-on Station 1 is yours. Stations 2 and 3 are on the projector. --- ## Station 1 · Find, fix, then break the fix ![w:1080](figures/station1.svg) ```sh cd lab/station1-find-and-fix && make inputs && make && ./check.sh # 3 FAIL flawfinder recparse.c ; cppcheck --enable=warning,style recparse.c export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # class key, revoked after class claude ``` --- ## Station 1 · What the analyzers say ``` $ gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c recparse.c # silent $ flawfinder --dataonly recparse.c recparse.c:47: [4] strcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows (CWE-120) recparse.c:21: [2] char: Statically-sized arrays can be improperly restricted recparse.c:28: [2] fopen: Check when opening files - can an attacker redirect it recparse.c:53: [2] memcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows (CWE-120) recparse.c:63: [2] memcpy: Does not check for buffer overflows (CWE-120) ``` | line | verdict | |---|---| | 47 | ✓ the bug it says it is | | 63 | ✓ a bug, but the cause is a **signed** `len` check six lines up | | 21, 28, 53 | ✗ noise | --- ## Station 1 · Debrief
* **First patch passed `check.sh`?** Usually. Passed `leak-name32`? Often not. * **Neighbor got the same patch?** Rarely. Same model, same prompt. * **Your 6th input?** `len == MAX_DATA` · truncated length · empty file · no NUL
A test suite is a finite set of counterexample searches. It proves *incorrect*. It cannot prove *correct*. **You** chose the property (no leak, not just no crash) and wrote the input. The agent cannot do that part.
--- ## Station 2 · An agent reads packets ![w:1080](figures/network.svg) --- ## Station 3 · An agent drives Ghidra ![w:1080](figures/ghidra.svg) --- # Part 4 · The contract What the agent does, what you do, and what neither gets to skip --- ## The contract ![w:1080](figures/contract.svg) > Undecidability is not a reason to avoid the tools. Next move? **A.** Merge it; the tests pass **B.** Ask the agent to confirm the fix is correct **C.** Write the input the tests don't cover, then read the diff **D.** Run it again and see if it gives the same patch --- ## Q3 → **C. Write the uncovered input, then read the diff** - **A** trusts a finite test suite to decide an undecidable property - **B** asks the proposer to be the judge - **D** tells you the model is unstable, not whether this patch is right - **C** is what you did at Station 1 --- ## References

definition.name: SendFeedback
definition.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
